text: Apple Black Rot. Black rot is a fungus disease of apple that causes purple frogeye spots on leaves, a firm black rot on fruit, and sunken cankers on branches. Dead wood and old fruit on the tree carry it from year to year.
source: Pome fruit disease: black rot and frogeye leaf spot (Penn State Extension)

text: Apple Black Rot symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves that grow bigger, with a brown or tan centre and a purple edge, like a frog's eye. Fruit rot usually starts at the blossom end as a brown spot, then forms brown and black rings while the flesh stays firm and leathery. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard black mummy that can hang on the tree for a year or more. Reddish-brown, sunken patches on bark that grow into cankers (dead areas) on limbs and branches, with twig dieback.
source: Pome fruit disease: black rot and frogeye leaf spot (Penn State Extension)

text: Apple Black Rot causes and spread: A fungus (Botryosphaeria obtusa, also called Diplodia seriata) that survives on cankers, dead bark, dead twigs and mummified fruit. Spores are spread by rain splash, wind and insects, mainly around petal fall, and enter leaves, fruit and wounds. Warm, wet weather, wounds from hail, insects or pruning, and stressed or winter-injured trees favour it. Wood killed by fire blight is an easy entry point.
source: Pome fruit disease: black rot and frogeye leaf spot (Penn State Extension)

text: Apple Black Rot what to do, treatment and control: Prune out cankers and dead wood, cutting well below the diseased area, and destroy the prunings by burying or burning them. Pick up and remove all mummified fruit from the trees and from the orchard floor. Remove shoots killed by fire blight, since the black rot fungus can live in them during the season. Keep trees healthy with regular pruning and balanced feeding, and avoid wounding trunks, limbs and fruit. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Pome fruit disease: black rot and frogeye leaf spot (Penn State Extension)

text: Apple Black Rot prevention: Do yearly sanitation: remove dead wood, cankers and mummies before spring. Keep trees vigorous and reduce stress, because weak trees get cankers more easily. Limit wounds from tools, insects and hail where possible, because wounds are the main entry point.
source: Pome fruit disease: black rot and frogeye leaf spot (Penn State Extension)

text: Apple Black Rot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if cankers keep spreading or many fruit rot despite sanitation.
source: Pome fruit disease: black rot and frogeye leaf spot (Penn State Extension)

text: Apple Mosaic Virus. Apple mosaic virus is a virus that causes pale or yellow patches on apple leaves, slows tree growth and lowers yield. It has no cure and spreads through infected planting material.
source: Apple Mosaic Virus (Utah State University Extension)

text: Apple Mosaic Virus symptoms: Pale, cream or yellow spots and random patches of yellowing on leaves as they open in spring. Slow tree growth and low fruit yield. Severely infected trees can set far fewer buds. Symptoms are stronger in some seasons, depending on spring temperatures.
source: Apple Mosaic Virus (Utah State University Extension)

text: Apple Mosaic Virus causes and spread: Apple mosaic virus, a virus living inside the leaves and shoots of the tree. It spreads when buds or twigs from an infected tree are grafted or budded onto healthy trees. Sources say insects and pollen do not spread it. Spread through natural root grafts is not considered important in orchards.
source: Apple Mosaic Virus (Utah State University Extension)

text: Apple Mosaic Virus what to do, treatment and control: Do not take buds or scion wood (twigs used for grafting) from infected trees. Plant only virus-free, certified trees from a trusted nursery. Mark trees showing mosaic and consider replacing badly affected ones with healthy stock, because there is no cure. Ask your agriculture officer to confirm the problem, since leaf yellowing can also come from other causes.
source: Apple Mosaic Virus (Utah State University Extension)

text: Apple Mosaic Virus prevention: Buy only certified virus-free planting material. Use virus-free scion wood for all grafting and budding. Keep infected trees out of any propagation block.
source: Apple Mosaic Virus (Utah State University Extension)

text: Apple Mosaic Virus when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer to confirm the diagnosis and to find a source of virus-free trees.
source: Apple Mosaic Virus (Utah State University Extension)

text: Apple Rust. Apple rust (cedar apple rust) is a fungus disease that makes yellow-orange spots on apple leaves and sometimes fruit. The fungus needs a second host, juniper or cedar trees, to complete its life cycle.
source: Cedar Apple Rust (University of Illinois Extension)

text: Apple Rust symptoms: Small yellow spots on leaves in spring that grow into yellow-orange spots with a red border and tiny black dots in the centre. Later in summer, small cup-like tufts form on the underside of the leaf, under each spot. Raised orange spots on fruit, which may crack and turn brown; infected stems can cause early fruit drop. On nearby juniper or cedar: brown galls (hard lumps) that grow orange, jelly-like horns in spring rain.
source: Cedar Apple Rust (University of Illinois Extension)

text: Apple Rust causes and spread: A fungus (Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae) that lives on two hosts: juniper or cedar, and apple. Spring rain swells the galls on juniper and wind carries spores to apple leaves and fruit. Wet spring weather favours infection. Spores from apple leaves go back to juniper, not to other apple trees, so there is no spread from apple to apple. In India this rust is not widely documented; the sources describe it from other countries.
source: Cedar Apple Rust (University of Illinois Extension)

text: Apple Rust what to do, treatment and control: Look for galls on any juniper or cedar near the orchard and remove them before the orange horns form in spring. Check young leaves in spring for yellow spots, especially in wet weather. Prefer resistant apple varieties when planting or replacing trees. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Cedar Apple Rust (University of Illinois Extension)

text: Apple Rust prevention: Plant apple varieties that are resistant to rust. Remove juniper and cedar trees near the orchard where practical; the closer they are, the worse the disease. Scout every spring during wet weather, from tight cluster to a few weeks after petal fall.
source: Cedar Apple Rust (University of Illinois Extension)

text: Apple Rust when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if you see orange spots on leaves or fruit, to confirm what it is.
source: Cedar Apple Rust (University of Illinois Extension)

text: Apple Scab. Apple scab is a fungus disease that spots leaves and fruit in cool, wet spring weather. It can cause heavy losses and leaves fruit rough, cracked and unsellable.
source: Apple Scab (eXtension Apples)

text: Apple Scab symptoms: Young leaf spots are velvety, olive green to brown, with feathery edges that become sharper with age. Badly infected young leaves thicken, curl, shrivel and drop. Fruit spots start like leaf spots, then turn brown and corky; early infection causes cracked, uneven, misshapen fruit. Late infection can show only in storage as small rough black spots.
source: Apple Scab (eXtension Apples)

text: Apple Scab causes and spread: A fungus (Venturia inaequalis) that survives winter mainly in fallen leaves and fruit on the orchard floor. Spores are released around bud break and through spring, and need wet leaves or fruit to infect. Rain splash and wind spread more spores from spots during the season. Cool, humid spring weather favours it.
source: Apple Scab (eXtension Apples)

text: Apple Scab what to do, treatment and control: Rake up or chop fallen leaves and fruit in late autumn so they rot faster and release fewer spores next spring. Check young leaves and fruit early in spring and keep scouting, to catch the disease before it spreads. Prune each year so the canopy dries quickly and spray, if used, covers well. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Apple Scab (eXtension Apples)

text: Apple Scab prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties where available. Choose a well-aired site and give trees enough spacing. Prune every year to open the canopy and shorten the time leaves stay wet. Do leaf-litter clean-up every autumn.
source: Apple Scab (eXtension Apples)

text: Apple Scab when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer for spray timing advice during wet spring weather.
source: Apple Scab (eXtension Apples)

text: Bell Pepper Bacterial Spot. A bacterial disease that causes dark leaf spots, early leaf drop and rough scab-like blisters on pepper fruit. It spreads fast in warm, wet weather.
source: Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Bacterial Spot symptoms: Water-soaked leaf spots, often with a yellow halo, that turn dark brown and can join into blighted patches. In dry weather, spots dry and fall out, leaving leaves tattered. Leaves yellow and drop early, exposing fruit to sunscald. Small raised blisters on fruit that turn brown and scab-like.
source: Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Bacterial Spot causes and spread: Bacteria of the Xanthomonas group cause it. They live on seed, diseased seedlings, volunteer plants and crop debris. Wind-driven rain, irrigation splash and handling wet plants spread them. Warm weather, high humidity and long leaf wetness favour it.
source: Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Bacterial Spot what to do, treatment and control: Remove and destroy infected seedlings and plants. Do not spray, tie, harvest or handle plants while they are wet. Remove nightshade-family weeds and volunteer plants from and near the field. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Plough or disk crop residue soon after the last harvest to help it rot.
source: Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Bacterial Spot prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and healthy seedlings, and reject infected ones. Use drip watering instead of overhead watering where possible. Choose resistant varieties suited to the strains in your area. Rotate for at least 3 years, and do not follow pepper with tomato, eggplant or potato.
source: Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Bacterial Spot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spots keep spreading, since no single step controls this disease.
source: Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Blossom End Rot. A disorder, not an infection, where the bottom end of the fruit turns brown and sunken. It comes from too little calcium reaching the fruit, linked to uneven watering.
source: Blossom-End Rot - New Mexico State University

text: Bell Pepper Blossom End Rot symptoms: A tan to brown spot on the blossom end of the fruit, the end opposite the stem. The spot grows and becomes sunken and leathery. Black or watery rot may follow when other fungi or bacteria invade the damaged spot. Affected fruit ripen faster than healthy fruit.
source: Blossom-End Rot - New Mexico State University

text: Bell Pepper Blossom End Rot causes and spread: It is a physiological disorder: calcium does not reach the developing fruit. It does not spread from plant to plant. Soil that is too wet or too dry, high salts, and too much nitrogen, magnesium, potassium or sodium fertiliser can block calcium uptake. Calcium moves slowly in the plant, so even a short water shortage in warm, fast-growing weather can trigger it.
source: Blossom-End Rot - New Mexico State University

text: Bell Pepper Blossom End Rot what to do, treatment and control: Water regularly so the root zone is never bone dry or waterlogged. Mulch the soil to keep moisture even and limit digging near the roots. Pick off and discard affected fruit so the plant puts energy into healthy ones. Do not over-fertilise; too much lush growth makes it worse. Have the soil tested, and ask your agriculture officer how to correct soil acidity or calcium if needed.
source: Blossom-End Rot - New Mexico State University

text: Bell Pepper Blossom End Rot prevention: Test the soil before planting and fix its acidity as advised. Plant in well-drained soil. Choose varieties more tolerant of the disorder; shorter, rounder peppers usually do better than long ones. Avoid deep cultivation that damages roots.
source: Blossom-End Rot - New Mexico State University

text: Bell Pepper Blossom End Rot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer for a soil test and advice if many fruit are affected season after season.
source: Blossom-End Rot - New Mexico State University

text: Bell Pepper Frogeye Leaf Spot. A fungal leaf spot of pepper that makes round spots with a pale centre and dark ring. Heavy leaf loss lowers yield and can expose fruit to sunburn.
source: Cercospora Leaf Spot (Frogeye Leaf Spot) on Pepper - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Frogeye Leaf Spot symptoms: Small round, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn tan to white with a darker ring. Spot centres dry out and crack or fall out. Long spots on stems that can girdle (ring) the stem. Leaves yellow and drop, leaving fruit open to sunscald.
source: Cercospora Leaf Spot (Frogeye Leaf Spot) on Pepper - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Frogeye Leaf Spot causes and spread: A fungus (Cercospora capsici, also called Passalora capsicicola) that survives on old crop debris between seasons. Infected seed and seedlings can carry it, and overhead watering is a risk. It prefers hot, humid weather with warm nights.
source: Cercospora Leaf Spot (Frogeye Leaf Spot) on Pepper - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Frogeye Leaf Spot what to do, treatment and control: Inspect seedlings and discard diseased ones before planting. Remove affected leaves early, and bury or destroy diseased plants. Use drip watering instead of watering over the leaves. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Cercospora Leaf Spot (Frogeye Leaf Spot) on Pepper - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Frogeye Leaf Spot prevention: Use disease-free seed. Rotate away from pepper, tomato and other nightshade crops for at least two years. Bury crop debris after harvest. Choose resistant pepper varieties where you have had the disease before.
source: Cercospora Leaf Spot (Frogeye Leaf Spot) on Pepper - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Frogeye Leaf Spot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if leaf spotting and leaf drop keep increasing.
source: Cercospora Leaf Spot (Frogeye Leaf Spot) on Pepper - NC State Extension

text: Bell Pepper Powdery Mildew. A fungal disease where white powder grows under pepper leaves and yellow patches show on top. Infected leaves drop, leaving fruit open to sunburn.
source: Powdery Mildew on Peppers - UC IPM

text: Bell Pepper Powdery Mildew symptoms: White powdery growth on the underside of leaves that turns brown with age. Yellow or brownish patches on the upper leaf surface above it. Leaf edges curl upward, showing the powder. Older leaves drop, exposing fruit to sunburn.
source: Powdery Mildew on Peppers - UC IPM

text: Bell Pepper Powdery Mildew causes and spread: A fungus (Leveillula taurica) that grows mostly inside the leaf and makes spores on the underside. It also infects tomato, eggplant, onion, cotton and many weeds. Wind spreads the spores and infection can repeat every 7 to 10 days. Infected seedlings may show nothing for 18 to 21 days. It develops across a wide range of warm temperatures; humidity helps spores germinate.
source: Powdery Mildew on Peppers - UC IPM

text: Bell Pepper Powdery Mildew what to do, treatment and control: Scout the undersides of leaves regularly, especially in warm weather, because early signs are easy to miss. Remove badly affected leaves or plants and clear weeds that can host the fungus. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Treatment works best early in the infection. Check seedlings for symptoms before planting, since the disease can arrive on transplants.
source: Powdery Mildew on Peppers - UC IPM

text: Bell Pepper Powdery Mildew prevention: Start with healthy seedlings from a trusted source. Keep the field and its edges free of weeds that host the fungus. Do not rely on field cleaning alone because the fungus has many hosts. Keep checking the crop through the warm season.
source: Powdery Mildew on Peppers - UC IPM

text: Bell Pepper Powdery Mildew when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if white powder or yellow patches appear on several plants.
source: Powdery Mildew on Peppers - UC IPM

text: Cherry Leaf Spot. Cherry leaf spot is a fungus disease that makes purple-brown spots and small holes in leaves. Badly hit trees lose leaves early, become weaker and give less fruit the next year.
source: Cherry leaf spot (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Cherry Leaf Spot symptoms: Purple spots on the upper side of older leaves in early summer, turning reddish-brown then brown. Nearby spots join into larger dead patches with yellow around them. Dead tissue falls out and leaves small holes, called a shothole look. Heavily infected leaves turn yellow and drop early; spots can also appear on leaf or fruit stalks.
source: Cherry leaf spot (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Cherry Leaf Spot causes and spread: A fungus (Blumeriella jaapii) that survives winter inside fallen infected leaves. In spring it releases spores that wind and splashing water carry to new leaves. Spores need wet leaves to infect. Frequent rain in spring and early summer and mild temperatures make it spread fast. Plums can also be affected.
source: Cherry leaf spot (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Cherry Leaf Spot what to do, treatment and control: Rake up and compost or remove fallen leaves in autumn to cut the spores available next spring. Check leaves from early summer and act quickly if leaves are dropping early. Keep trees healthy, since early leaf loss makes trees prone to winter injury and low fruit set. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Cherry leaf spot (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Cherry Leaf Spot prevention: Clean up fallen leaves every autumn. Scout every year from early summer, because the disease returns where leaves were left. Combine sanitation with any spray programme advised locally, as sprays work best that way.
source: Cherry leaf spot (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Cherry Leaf Spot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if trees lose most of their leaves early in the season.
source: Cherry leaf spot (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Cherry Powdery Mildew. Powdery mildew is a fungus disease that makes white powdery patches on the underside of young cherry leaves. Bad attacks distort leaves, cause early leaf fall and can mark the fruit.
source: Cherry Powdery Mildew in Utah

text: Cherry Powdery Mildew symptoms: Small white powdery patches on the underside of young leaves, which are easy to miss at first. Leaves can pucker, curl at the edges, turn brittle, bronze or die in spots, and fall early. Sweet cherry fruit can become rough and russeted or get a dull whitish coating. Fast, soft shoots and suckers are attacked first.
source: Cherry Powdery Mildew in Utah

text: Cherry Powdery Mildew causes and spread: A fungus that survives the winter as tiny fruiting bodies on fallen infected leaves and, to a lesser extent, in bark cracks. In spring, rain or irrigation releases spores that blow onto young leaves. Spores from the white patches then cause new infections about every week. Warm dry days with cool humid nights, crowded canopies, soft new growth and too much nitrogen fertiliser favour it. Old leaves resist infection.
source: Cherry Powdery Mildew in Utah

text: Cherry Powdery Mildew what to do, treatment and control: Check young leaves, especially on suckers and low spurs, from early in the season. Look at the underside of leaves in good light. Thin out dense branches so air moves through the tree and leaves dry faster. Cut off suckers in spring because their soft leaves are very easily infected. Rake up and destroy fallen leaves late in the season, since the fungus overwinters on them. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Cherry Powdery Mildew in Utah

text: Cherry Powdery Mildew prevention: Avoid too much nitrogen fertiliser that pushes soft, lush growth. Choose varieties that show some resistance where available; some sweet cherry types are much more susceptible than others. Prune every year to keep the canopy open and the tree at a size you can reach and inspect.
source: Cherry Powdery Mildew in Utah

text: Cherry Powdery Mildew when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if white powdery growth keeps returning or spreads to fruit.
source: Cherry Powdery Mildew in Utah

text: Corn Gray Leaf Spot. A fungus disease of corn leaves that makes long rectangular tan to gray spots between the veins. Heavy attack on the leaves above the ear can cut yield.
source: Gray Leaf Spot on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Gray Leaf Spot symptoms: Early spots are small brown or tan spots with yellow edges, easiest to see when the leaf is held to the light. Older spots are tan to gray, rectangular with blunt ends, and stopped by the leaf veins. In severe cases spots join and whole leaves, even whole plants, dry up. Stalks may weaken and fall over in severe cases, and the field may ripen early.
source: Gray Leaf Spot on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Gray Leaf Spot causes and spread: Caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis, which survives on corn residue lying on or above the soil and survives poorly when buried. Spores travel by wind and rain splash to lower leaves, and can blow in from nearby fields. Favoured by long leaf wetness, high humidity inside the crop, and moderate to warm weather. Risk is higher with susceptible hybrids, corn grown year after year, late planting and minimum tillage.
source: Gray Leaf Spot on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Gray Leaf Spot what to do, treatment and control: Walk the field and check lower leaves before flowering, especially if the field had this disease last season. After harvest, plough or bury corn residue so the fungus has less place to survive. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Avoid planting corn again in a field that had heavy disease; rotate to another crop.
source: Gray Leaf Spot on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Gray Leaf Spot prevention: Choose the most tolerant hybrids or varieties available; none is fully resistant. Rotate with a crop that is not corn. Avoid late planting. Bury residue after a diseased crop.
source: Gray Leaf Spot on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Gray Leaf Spot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spots are spreading on leaves above the ear.
source: Gray Leaf Spot on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Northern Leaf Blight. A fungus disease that makes long canoe-shaped spots on corn leaves. It is worst in damp, moderate weather and can cause losses in susceptible varieties.
source: Northern Corn Leaf Blight - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Northern Leaf Blight symptoms: Long canoe-shaped spots, about 1 to 6 inches long, on the leaves. Spots start gray-green at the edges, then turn tan and may show dark fungal growth. Spots appear first on lower leaves and then move upward. In severe cases leaves are blighted (dried up) quickly.
source: Northern Corn Leaf Blight - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Northern Leaf Blight causes and spread: Caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum; there are several races that behave differently on different varieties. The fungus survives on old corn leaf residue. Favoured by moderate temperatures (about 64 to 80 degrees F) and long periods of moisture. It usually shows at or after silking; earlier infection causes more damage.
source: Northern Corn Leaf Blight - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Northern Leaf Blight what to do, treatment and control: Check lower leaves for canoe-shaped spots, especially in damp weather before and around silking. Bury or clear old corn residue after harvest, since the fungus survives on it. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Rotate fields out of corn where the disease was heavy.
source: Northern Corn Leaf Blight - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Northern Leaf Blight prevention: Plant resistant hybrids or varieties; this is the main control. Rotate crops and manage residue after a diseased crop.
source: Northern Corn Leaf Blight - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Northern Leaf Blight when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spots appear on many plants before silking.
source: Northern Corn Leaf Blight - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Rust. A fungus disease that puts rusty-brown raised pustules on corn leaves. It is usually mild but can hurt the crop in long cool, wet spells.
source: Common Rust on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Rust symptoms: Small brown pustules (raised spots) on both the upper and lower leaf surfaces, and on leaf sheaths. Pustules are brick-red to cinnamon-brown and the powder rubs off on your fingers. Pustules darken as they age, often with a yellow ring around them. In severe attacks leaves turn yellow and die.
source: Common Rust on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Rust causes and spread: Caused by the rust fungus Puccinia sorghi. Its spores are carried by wind and new spores form within 7 to 14 days. Favoured by cool, moist weather (about 16 to 25 degrees C), heavy dew and at least 6 hours of wet leaves. Hot, dry weather slows or stops the disease. Young leaves are most easily infected.
source: Common Rust on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Rust what to do, treatment and control: Scout fields early and often, more so if rust has been seen in nearby fields. Note how much of the leaf is covered and how far the plants have grown, and show this to your agriculture officer. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Common Rust on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Rust prevention: Plant resistant hybrids or varieties where available; this is the cheapest control. Keep a watch on the crop in cool, wet weather.
source: Common Rust on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Rust when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if most leaves carry pustules before the crop is near maturity.
source: Common Rust on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Smut. A fungus disease that makes swollen, fleshy galls (tumour-like growths) on ears, tassels, stalks and leaves of corn. Dark spore powder fills the galls when they dry.
source: Common Smut on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Smut symptoms: Thick, fleshy galls, first covered in a white to silvery skin, on ears, stalks, tassels or leaves. Galls on leaves usually stay small and look like blisters. As galls ripen they turn dark inside, then dry and burst, releasing black dusty spores. Early infection can cause yellowing and rippling of leaf tissue near the galls.
source: Common Smut on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Smut causes and spread: Caused by the fungus Ustilago maydis. Its thick-walled spores live for several years in soil and crop residue. Wind and splashing rain or irrigation water carry spores to plants; the fungus enters through wounds or silks. Hail, wind or machine damage to young plants, and heat or drought that gives poor pollination, make it worse. Too much nitrogen fertilizer and wet weather can also favour it.
source: Common Smut on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Smut what to do, treatment and control: Check ears, tassels and stalks for galls. Field corn rarely loses much, so do not overspend on control. Take care not to wound young plants during weeding and other field work, because wounds let the fungus in. Rotate to another crop and keep soil fertility balanced; avoid too much nitrogen.
source: Common Smut on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Smut prevention: Plant resistant hybrids or varieties where available. Rotate crops and keep soil fertility balanced; avoid excess nitrogen. Clear crop residue after harvest.
source: Common Smut on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Corn Smut when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if many ears in the field carry galls.
source: Common Smut on Corn - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Peach Anthracnose. Anthracnose of peach is a fungus rot of ripening fruit. It starts as small round sunken spots that stay firm, and in humid weather orange spore masses ooze out in rings.
source: Anthracnose Fruit Rot of Peach (University of Kentucky Fruit Scout)

text: Peach Anthracnose symptoms: Small, round, sunken spots on fruit that stay firm as they grow, unlike brown rot. In wet or humid weather, salmon or orange coloured spore masses ooze from the spots in rings. Symptoms appear only when fruit is ripe or nearly ripe, even though infection happened much earlier.
source: Anthracnose Fruit Rot of Peach (University of Kentucky Fruit Scout)

text: Peach Anthracnose causes and spread: A Colletotrichum fungus. The fungus survives the winter on diseased fruit and infected twigs. Infection happens soon after blossom time, but the rot shows only as fruit ripens. Wet, humid weather brings out the spore masses and spreads the disease.
source: Anthracnose Fruit Rot of Peach (University of Kentucky Fruit Scout)

text: Peach Anthracnose what to do, treatment and control: Pick off and destroy infected fruit and cut out diseased twigs, and dispose of them away from the orchard. Prune and thin the tree so air moves through and fruit and leaves dry quickly. Do not leave fallen or rotten fruit under trees because they carry the fungus to the next season. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Anthracnose Fruit Rot of Peach (University of Kentucky Fruit Scout)

text: Peach Anthracnose prevention: Prune, thin and space trees every year for good airflow. Keep the orchard clean of old fruit and dead twigs. Check fruit and twigs each season so you can tell this rot from brown rot early.
source: Anthracnose Fruit Rot of Peach (University of Kentucky Fruit Scout)

text: Peach Anthracnose when to get help: Ask your agriculture extension officer to confirm whether fruit spots are anthracnose or brown rot before you act.
source: Anthracnose Fruit Rot of Peach (University of Kentucky Fruit Scout)

text: Peach Brown Rot. Brown rot is a fungus disease that kills peach blossoms and twigs and rots ripening fruit into dry, wrinkled mummies. It is worst in warm, wet weather.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Brown Rot symptoms: Blossoms turn brown, wither and die, often covered with a brownish-gray mass of spores. Fruit gets soft brown spots that spread fast and bear tan, powdery spore masses. Rotted fruit dries into a wrinkled mummy that often stays hanging on the tree. Twigs can form cankers (dead sunken patches) with gum, and leaves on those twigs may brown and wither.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Brown Rot causes and spread: A fungus (Monilinia fructicola) that survives the winter in mummified fruit on the ground or tree and in cankers from the last season. Spores spread by wind, rain splash and insects. They need a film of water on the plant for at least 5 hours to infect. Wounds from insects, hail, cracking or rough handling let the fungus in, and fruit touching each other pass it on. Wet weather with moderate temperatures favours it.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Brown Rot what to do, treatment and control: Pick up and destroy dropped and rotted fruit, and remove mummies from the tree. Prune out cankers and blighted twigs in the dormant season and destroy them by burning or deep burial. Control insects that feed on fruit, and handle ripe fruit gently to avoid cuts and bruises. Remove wild or neglected stone fruit trees nearby that harbour the fungus. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Brown Rot prevention: Keep the orchard floor and packing area free of rotten fruit. Cool harvested fruit quickly and store it cold. Choose varieties with better resistance when you can.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Brown Rot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if blossoms or fruit rot every season despite sanitation.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Leaf Curl. Peach leaf curl is a fungus disease that makes new leaves thick, twisted and reddish in spring. Badly hit leaves turn pale and fall, which weakens the tree.
source: Peach Leaf Curl (West Virginia University Extension)

text: Peach Leaf Curl symptoms: Reddish areas on young leaves in early spring that thicken, pucker and curl. Thick areas turn pale yellow and then grayish white as spores form on them. Affected leaves turn brown or yellow and may drop, so the tree loses vigour and fruit. Young shoots can be stunted or twisted, and rarely fruit shows red, wrinkled, corky patches.
source: Peach Leaf Curl (West Virginia University Extension)

text: Peach Leaf Curl causes and spread: The fungus Taphrina deformans. It survives on twigs, in bark cracks and around buds. Wind and rain wash spores onto swelling buds and opening leaves in early spring. Cool, wet weather with high humidity at bud swell and leaf opening favours infection. Warm weather with fast leaf growth rarely allows it.
source: Peach Leaf Curl (West Virginia University Extension)

text: Peach Leaf Curl what to do, treatment and control: Note the trees and branches affected this year. Once leaves are curled, the damage for this season cannot be undone. Help weakened trees by thinning fruit, watering during dry spells and feeding the tree sensibly. Prune in the dormant season and remove fallen curled leaves to cut the spores that carry over. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Peach Leaf Curl (West Virginia University Extension)

text: Peach Leaf Curl prevention: Plant peach or nectarine varieties that tolerate leaf curl where available. Keep trees vigorous with pruning, feeding and watering. Plan protection before bud swell next season, not after leaves have curled, and ask your officer about timing.
source: Peach Leaf Curl (West Virginia University Extension)

text: Peach Leaf Curl when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer before bud swell to plan timing for next season, because curled leaves cannot be cured.
source: Peach Leaf Curl (West Virginia University Extension)

text: Peach Rust. Peach rust is a fungus disease that causes bright yellow angular spots on the upper side of leaves and rusty brown spore masses underneath. It can cause early leaf fall and spotted fruit.
source: Peach Rust (UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines)

text: Peach Rust symptoms: Bright yellow, angular spots on the upper leaf surface. Brown to reddish-brown spore masses on the underside of the leaf. Early attacks can cause leaves to fall in mid-season. Small brownish spots with green halos on fruit, which become sunken as the fruit ripens. Small cankers (bark splits) on twigs in spring.
source: Peach Rust (UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines)

text: Peach Rust causes and spread: The rust fungus Tranzschelia discolor. It survives the winter in twig lesions. Spores from twigs infect leaves in spring, and leaf spores then infect fruit and twigs. Spores need wetness to infect. Heavy or late rain, sprinkler or flood irrigation that wets leaves, and damp air from weeds or nearby water favour it. Fruit is most at risk when nearly full size.
source: Peach Rust (UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines)

text: Peach Rust what to do, treatment and control: If you use sprinklers, aim them low or shield them so leaves are not wetted. Check fruit every second week after colour starts to change, so you spot rust early. Keep weeds and low vegetation under trees cut down so air stays drier around the tree. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Peach Rust (UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines)

text: Peach Rust prevention: Use drip irrigation instead of flood, furrow or sprinkler irrigation where you can. Avoid planting in damp, low spots near standing water. Keep the orchard floor weed free to reduce humidity.
source: Peach Rust (UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines)

text: Peach Rust when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if leaves fall early in mid-season or fruit spots appear.
source: Peach Rust (UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines)

text: Peach Scab. Peach scab is a fungus disease that makes olive-green to black velvety spots on fruit, twigs and leaves. The skin may crack, and bad attacks cause small, distorted fruit.
source: Peach Scab (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Scab symptoms: Small round olive-green spots on fruit, mostly near the stem end on the sunny side, that can join into dark velvety blotches. Severe attack can stunt or distort fruit, crack the skin and cause early fruit drop. Small yellowish spots on leaves that can fall out and leave shot-holes, with early leaf drop in wet seasons. Twig spots are slightly raised, round to oval and brown, and infected twigs can die back.
source: Peach Scab (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Scab causes and spread: A fungus (Cladosporium carpophilum) that survives the winter as spots on twigs infected the previous year. Spores form on twig spots and are splashed or blown by rain and mist onto fruit and leaves from about shuck fall. Spots show 40 to 70 days later. Wet spring and early summer weather, warm humid days, and low, shaded sites with poor airflow favour it.
source: Peach Scab (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Scab what to do, treatment and control: Cut out and destroy scabby twigs before spring growth starts. Remove or destroy wild or neglected peach, plum and apricot trees nearby. Prune to open the canopy so fruit and leaves dry faster after rain. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Lightly spotted fruit is only skin deep, and peeling makes it fit to eat or process.
source: Peach Scab (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Scab prevention: Avoid planting in low, shaded spots with poor drainage and air movement. Prune every year to keep air moving through the tree. Keep nearby stone fruit trees clean of disease.
source: Peach Scab (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Peach Scab when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if scab spots appear on most of the fruit in your orchard.
source: Peach Scab (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

text: Plum Bacterial Spot. Bacterial spot is a disease caused by bacteria that spots plum leaves, fruit and twigs. Leaves get angular spots and shot-holes, and fruit can pit, crack and become unmarketable.
source: Bacterial spot of peach and plum (Michigan State University Extension)

text: Plum Bacterial Spot symptoms: Angular yellowing or dead spots on leaves, often with yellow halos, whose centres fall out to leave a shot-hole look. Severe attack makes leaves fall early. Fruit gets purple-black flecks, pits, cracks and gum, and spotted fruit rots more easily. Small gummy, water-soaked cankers on twigs in spring can girdle them and kill the tips.
source: Bacterial spot of peach and plum (Michigan State University Extension)

text: Plum Bacterial Spot causes and spread: A bacterium, Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni, that survives the winter in diseased twigs. In spring it spreads from cankers by splashing rain and insects. Wind-blown sand and sprayer wind create small wounds that help it enter. Rain, dew, high humidity and wet leaves favour infection. Fruit is most at risk from shuck split until pit hardening.
source: Bacterial spot of peach and plum (Michigan State University Extension)

text: Plum Bacterial Spot what to do, treatment and control: Cut out gummy, blackened twig tips in spring pruning and destroy them to reduce the bacteria. Rake up and destroy fallen leaves. Prune to open the canopy for air circulation. Check leaves in light from spring through mid-summer, especially near the main veins. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Bacterial spot of peach and plum (Michigan State University Extension)

text: Plum Bacterial Spot prevention: Plant varieties with better resistance, especially on sandy sites. Put susceptible varieties inside the block and resistant ones on the exposed edge, and plant windbreak trees on the windward side. Use sod strips between trees and control dust from nearby dirt roads.
source: Bacterial spot of peach and plum (Michigan State University Extension)

text: Plum Bacterial Spot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if twig cankers or leaf spots keep returning each season.
source: Bacterial spot of peach and plum (Michigan State University Extension)

text: Plum Brown Rot. Brown rot is a fungus disease that kills plum blossoms and twigs and rots ripening fruit into dry, wrinkled mummies. It is worst in warm, wet weather.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (University of Nebraska Extension G1965)

text: Plum Brown Rot symptoms: Blossoms turn brown, wither and die, often covered with a brownish-gray mass of spores. Fruit gets soft brown spots that spread fast and bear tan, powdery spore masses. Rotted fruit dries into a wrinkled mummy that often stays hanging on the tree. Twigs can form cankers (dead sunken patches) with gum, and leaves on those twigs may brown and wither.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (University of Nebraska Extension G1965)

text: Plum Brown Rot causes and spread: A fungus (Monilinia fructicola) that survives the winter in mummified fruit on the ground or tree and in cankers from the last season. Spores spread by wind, rain splash and insects such as bees and beetles, and infect after a film of water has stayed on the plant for at least 5 hours. Wounds from insects, hail or rough handling let the fungus in, and fruit touching each other pass it on. Symptoms are similar across stone fruits.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (University of Nebraska Extension G1965)

text: Plum Brown Rot what to do, treatment and control: Pick up and destroy dropped and rotted fruit, and remove mummies from the tree. Prune out cankers in the dormant season and destroy them by burning or deep burial. Control insects that feed on fruit and handle ripe fruit gently to avoid punctures and bruises. Remove wild or neglected stone fruit trees nearby that harbour the fungus. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (University of Nebraska Extension G1965)

text: Plum Brown Rot prevention: Keep the orchard floor and packing area free of rotten fruit. Cool harvested fruit quickly after picking. Choose varieties with better resistance when you can.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (University of Nebraska Extension G1965)

text: Plum Brown Rot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if blossoms or fruit rot every season despite sanitation.
source: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (University of Nebraska Extension G1965)

text: Plum Pocket Disease. Plum pocket is a fungus disease in which a few plums swell to many times normal size, turn spongy and hollow, and have no stone. The tree itself is usually not harmed.
source: Plum pockets (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Plum Pocket Disease symptoms: A small blister forms on young fruit soon after flowering and quickly spreads over the whole plum. The fruit swells to about ten times its normal size, feels spongy and gets covered with velvety gray spores. Later the fruit dries out and turns black, and it is hollow in the centre when cut. Leaves may thicken and curl, but this is uncommon. Usually only a few fruit on a tree are affected.
source: Plum pockets (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Plum Pocket Disease causes and spread: The fungus Taphrina communis. Wind and rain carry spores to fruit as it develops. The spores survive the winter on twigs and bud scales and infect again the following spring. Cool, wet weather during bud break and early fruit growth favours infection.
source: Plum pockets (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Plum Pocket Disease what to do, treatment and control: Remove infected plums from the tree before they are covered with spores. Bury infected fruit in a compost pile or deep in the soil, away from the orchard. Promote tree health with pruning, feeding and watering. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Plum pockets (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Plum Pocket Disease prevention: Plant resistant varieties where available. Keep trees vigorous with good pruning, feeding and watering. Remove fallen and mummified fruit before spring.
source: Plum pockets (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Plum Pocket Disease when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if many plums on your trees are affected year after year.
source: Plum pockets (University of Minnesota Extension)

text: Plum Pox Virus. Plum pox (also called sharka) is a virus disease of plum and other stone fruit trees. It marks leaves and fruit and makes fruit drop early. It cannot be cured, so infected trees must be removed.
source: Plum Pox: A New Threat to Stone Fruit Production in the United States (Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station)

text: Plum Pox Virus symptoms: Pale green spots, rings, lines or yellow veins on leaves, often seen only in early summer. Plum fruit can show rings or blotches, become pocked and deformed with sunken rings, and drop early. Red rings and spots on plum stones, visible when the fruit is cut open. Some infected trees show no clear symptoms for up to 3 years, and symptoms may fade in hot weather.
source: Plum Pox: A New Threat to Stone Fruit Production in the United States (Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station)

text: Plum Pox Virus causes and spread: Plum Pox Virus, a virus spread over long distances by infected budwood, rootstocks and nursery plants, which may show no symptoms. Within an orchard, winged aphids carry it from tree to tree. Suckers from infected rootstocks and root grafts can also carry it. Many wild and ornamental Prunus trees can carry the virus and act as sources.
source: Plum Pox: A New Threat to Stone Fruit Production in the United States (Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station)

text: Plum Pox Virus what to do, treatment and control: Report any suspected infected tree to your agriculture officer without delay, because the virus cannot be cured and the tree must be tested. Remove infected trees promptly, including roots and suckers, as advised by your officer. Do not let aphids feed on trees waiting to be removed, since they can still spread the virus. Dispose of cull fruit away from healthy orchards, and control weeds in and near the orchard.
source: Plum Pox: A New Threat to Stone Fruit Production in the United States (Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station)

text: Plum Pox Virus prevention: Buy only virus-free, certified trees and budwood from trusted nurseries. Do not move plant material from infected areas. Do not rely on insecticides to stop the spread, because aphids can pass the virus quickly. Check trees each season and test leaf samples, since looking alone misses infections.
source: Plum Pox: A New Threat to Stone Fruit Production in the United States (Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station)

text: Plum Pox Virus when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer at once if you suspect plum pox, because infected trees can spread it to your whole orchard.
source: Plum Pox: A New Threat to Stone Fruit Production in the United States (Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station)

text: Plum Rust. Plum rust is a fungus disease that makes yellow spots on the upper side of leaves and brown spore pustules on the underside. Bad attacks make leaves yellow and fall.
source: Prune and Plum (Prunus spp.) - Rust (Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks)

text: Plum Rust symptoms: Yellow spots on the upper leaf surface. Brown spore pustules (small raised dots) on the underside of the leaf. Infected leaves take a yellowish cast and may drop in large numbers. Symptoms become more common toward the end of summer.
source: Prune and Plum (Prunus spp.) - Rust (Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks)

text: Plum Rust causes and spread: Rust fungi (Tranzschelia discolor and Tranzschelia pruni-spinosae). Anemone plants are an alternate host for one of them. The fungus survives the winter in twig lesions. Spores from twigs infect leaves in spring, and leaf spores then infect fruit and twigs. Spread continues while leaves stay wet or the air is humid. Abundant or late rain and sprinkler irrigation that wets leaves favour it.
source: Prune and Plum (Prunus spp.) - Rust (Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks)

text: Plum Rust what to do, treatment and control: Check leaves on the underside for brown pustules, especially late in the season. Use drip irrigation, or aim sprinklers low or shield them so leaves are not wetted. Cut down weeds and low plants under the trees to reduce humidity around the tree. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Prune and Plum (Prunus spp.) - Rust (Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks)

text: Plum Rust prevention: Prefer drip irrigation over flood, furrow or sprinkler irrigation. Avoid damp, low spots near standing water for planting. Keep the orchard floor weed free.
source: Prune and Plum (Prunus spp.) - Rust (Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks)

text: Plum Rust when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if leaves yellow and drop early in the season.
source: Prune and Plum (Prunus spp.) - Rust (Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks)

text: Potato Early Blight. A fungal disease that causes brown, ring-patterned spots on potato leaves and sunken spots on tubers. Older leaves are hit first.
source: Early Blight or Alternaria Leaf Spot - University of Illinois Extension

text: Potato Early Blight symptoms: Round to angular brown spots on older leaves, with dark rings like a target. Infected leaves turn yellow, wither and drop. Dark velvety spore growth on the spots. Depressed, similar spots on tubers.
source: Early Blight or Alternaria Leaf Spot - University of Illinois Extension

text: Potato Early Blight causes and spread: A fungus (Alternaria solani) that survives in infected plant debris in or on the soil and on seed. Wind and splashing rain carry the spores. Heavy dew, rain and mild temperatures favour spore production and repeat infections. Plants stressed by poor fertility, drought or insect damage are hit harder.
source: Early Blight or Alternaria Leaf Spot - University of Illinois Extension

text: Potato Early Blight what to do, treatment and control: Scout older leaves for ringed spots, especially after dew or rain. Remove and destroy badly infected plant debris away from the field. Keep the crop well fed and watered so plants are not stressed. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Early Blight or Alternaria Leaf Spot - University of Illinois Extension

text: Potato Early Blight prevention: Rotate crops and plough in crop remains so fewer spores are near the new crop. Use healthy, disease-free seed tubers. Remove volunteer potato and tomato plants. Reduce plant stress from drought, poor fertility and insects.
source: Early Blight or Alternaria Leaf Spot - University of Illinois Extension

text: Potato Early Blight when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spotting spreads quickly or tubers show sunken spots.
source: Early Blight or Alternaria Leaf Spot - University of Illinois Extension

text: Potato Late Blight. A very fast disease of potato leaves, stems and tubers, caused by a water mould. It thrives in cool, wet weather and can destroy a crop quickly.
source: Late Blight on Tomatoes and Potatoes - UMass Amherst

text: Potato Late Blight symptoms: Large olive-green to brown spots on leaves, often with fuzzy white growth underneath in humid weather. Brown to blackish spots on stems. Leaves dry up and plants can die; vines may rot with a bad smell. Plants may collapse so fast they look frost-damaged.
source: Late Blight on Tomatoes and Potatoes - UMass Amherst

text: Potato Late Blight causes and spread: A water mould (Phytophthora infestans), the same organism behind the Irish potato famine, causes it. It survives in infected tubers kept as seed, cull piles, volunteer potatoes and nightshade weeds. Wind and wind-driven rain carry the spores far. Cool, wet and cloudy weather favours it; hot, dry periods do not.
source: Late Blight on Tomatoes and Potatoes - UMass Amherst

text: Potato Late Blight what to do, treatment and control: Remove infected plants, bag them and bury them deep or throw them away. Do not compost. Destroy volunteer potato plants and do not leave cull potato piles near the field. Scout the crop often in cool, wet weather, checking both sides of leaves and the stems. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Spraying works best before symptoms appear. Avoid watering over the leaves.
source: Late Blight on Tomatoes and Potatoes - UMass Amherst

text: Potato Late Blight prevention: Buy certified seed tubers and inspect them before planting; do not replant last year's tubers. Control nightshade-family weeds near the field. Choose resistant varieties where available. Give plants space so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew.
source: Late Blight on Tomatoes and Potatoes - UMass Amherst

text: Potato Late Blight when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer at once if you see these spots in cool, wet weather.
source: Late Blight on Tomatoes and Potatoes - UMass Amherst

text: Rice Blast. A fungus disease that burns rice leaves and can break the neck of the panicle (grain head), so grain is lost. It can attack at any growth stage from nursery to heading.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Blast

text: Rice Blast symptoms: Small bluish-green flecks on leaves grow into spindle-shaped spots with grey centres and dark brown edges. Spots join together and large patches of leaf dry up, so a badly hit nursery or field looks burnt. Black spots ring the nodes (joints) of the stem, and the stem may break at the node. Neck of the panicle turns grayish-brown to black, shrivels, and the panicle may fall over. Infection before the milky stage gives no grain. Later infection gives poor quality grain.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Blast

text: Rice Blast causes and spread: Caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae (also called Pyricularia grisea); its spores are in the air through the year. Favoured by cloudy skies, drizzle and frequent rain, wet leaves, high humidity and temperatures of about 25 to 28 degrees C. Too much nitrogen fertilizer, dry nurseries and late planting make the disease worse.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Blast

text: Rice Blast what to do, treatment and control: Check nursery and field often. Look for leaf spots at tillering and for neck infection at flowering. Give nitrogen fertilizer in split doses and avoid applying too much at one time. Remove weeds on bunds and field edges, which can carry the fungus. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. After harvest, clear straw and stubble from the field so the fungus does not carry over.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Blast

text: Rice Blast prevention: Grow resistant or tolerant varieties; this is the most practical and cheapest control. Ask your agriculture office which varieties suit your area. Avoid dry nurseries and avoid planting late. Avoid heavy nitrogen fertilizer; use split doses.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Blast

text: Rice Blast when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if leaf spots are spreading or if necks are turning black near flowering.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Blast

text: Rice Sheath Blight. A fungus disease of rice that starts on the leaf sheaths near the water line and climbs up the plant. Bad infection kills leaves and gives poorly filled grain.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Sheath Blight

text: Rice Sheath Blight symptoms: First spots are greenish-grey, oval or irregular, on the leaf sheath close to the water level. Spots grow with greyish-white centres and blackish-brown or purple-brown borders. Lesions join and spread upward from the water line towards the flag leaf (the top leaf). Many large lesions can kill whole leaves; in severe cases the whole plant dies. Heavy infection at heading and grain filling gives poorly filled grain, especially in the lower part of the panicle.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Sheath Blight

text: Rice Sheath Blight causes and spread: Caused by the fungus Rhizoctonia solani, which survives as hard round brown bodies (sclerotia) in soil and floats on irrigation water. Spreads through irrigation water; it can survive many months in soil and attacks many other plants. Favoured by humid weather (96 to 100 percent), temperatures of 28 to 32 degrees C, frequent rain, heavy nitrogen fertilizer and close spacing or high seed rate.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Sheath Blight

text: Rice Sheath Blight what to do, treatment and control: Do not let irrigation water flow from an infected field into healthy fields. Check the crop from tillering onward, looking at the sheaths near the water line. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. After harvest, plough deeply in summer and clear stubble to reduce the fungus left in the field.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Sheath Blight

text: Rice Sheath Blight prevention: Grow moderately resistant varieties; ask your agriculture office which ones suit your area. Avoid very close spacing and very high seed rates. Avoid too much nitrogen fertilizer. Add well rotted farmyard manure or other organic matter as advised locally.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Sheath Blight

text: Rice Sheath Blight when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if sheath lesions are climbing up the plants.
source: TNAU Agritech Portal - Rice Sheath Blight

text: Soybean Bacterial Blight. A bacterial disease that makes small angular spots with yellow halos on soybean leaves. It usually stays at low levels and seldom cuts yield much.
source: Bacterial Blight on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Bacterial Blight symptoms: Small angular water-soaked spots that turn yellow, then brown, as the leaf tissue dies. Dark spots are ringed by a yellowish-green halo. Spots join into large dead patches, and the dead tissue may fall out, leaving ragged leaves. Seen most on young leaves in the upper part of the plant. Stems, pods and seed can also be infected.
source: Bacterial Blight on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Bacterial Blight causes and spread: Caused by a bacterium, Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea (also written Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. glycinea). It survives in crop residue and can be carried on seed. Wind and rain spread it, and so does working in the field while leaves are wet. Cool, wet, windy weather favours it; hot, dry weather stops it.
source: Bacterial Blight on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Bacterial Blight what to do, treatment and control: Do not walk through or work in the field while the leaves are wet. Check young upper leaves after windy, rainy spells for angular spots with yellow halos. Do not save seed from a field that had this disease. Chemical sprays are not the main answer; ask your agriculture officer if the disease is severe.
source: Bacterial Blight on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Bacterial Blight prevention: Use clean, disease-free seed. Plant resistant varieties. Rotate with crops such as corn or small grains, which this bacterium does not infect. Bury or clear crop residue after a diseased crop.
source: Bacterial Blight on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Bacterial Blight when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if the disease returns in most seasons or is severe.
source: Bacterial Blight on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Brown Spot. A common fungus leaf disease of soybean, also called Septoria brown spot. It starts on lower leaves, can make leaves drop early, and seldom causes big yield loss.
source: Septoria Brown Spot in Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Brown Spot symptoms: Small dark brown spots on the lowest leaves first, which later move up the plant. Spots grow and join into irregular brown patches, often with yellow areas beside them. Leaves turn yellow, then rusty brown, and may drop early. Spots can also be seen on stems and pods. It can look like soybean rust, but brown spot has no raised pustules or spores under the leaf.
source: Septoria Brown Spot in Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Brown Spot causes and spread: Caused by the fungus Septoria glycines, which lives on soybean residue left from the last crop and may travel on seed. Spores are moved by wind and splashing rain. Favoured by warm, wet weather with at least 6 hours of leaf wetness. Worse when soybean is grown year after year in the same field, especially with little ploughing.
source: Septoria Brown Spot in Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Brown Spot what to do, treatment and control: Check lower leaves early in the season and see whether spots are climbing up the plant. If the disease is heavy, bury soybean residue after harvest so it rots faster. Rotate out of soybean for at least one year in fields where the disease keeps getting worse. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Septoria Brown Spot in Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Brown Spot prevention: Rotate soybean with other crops, not other legumes. Bury crop residue in fields with heavy infection. Pick varieties that tolerate the disease better; none is fully resistant.
source: Septoria Brown Spot in Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Brown Spot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if you cannot tell brown spot from soybean rust.
source: Septoria Brown Spot in Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Downy Mildew. A disease caused by a fungus-like organism that makes pale yellow spots on top of soybean leaves and grey fuzzy growth underneath. It is usually harmless to yield.
source: Downy Mildew on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Downy Mildew symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper side of young leaves, which are not water-soaked. Old spots merge into large irregular brown patches with yellow-green edges. Tan to gray fuzzy tufts on the underside of the leaf, mostly in humid, wet weather such as early morning. Infected seed may be small, dull white or cracked, with a whitish crust of spores inside the pod.
source: Downy Mildew on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Downy Mildew causes and spread: Caused by Peronospora manshurica, a fungus-like organism (an oomycete). It survives on infected leaves and on seed, and seed can carry it to the next crop. Dew, high humidity and mild temperatures favour it, and it is most common once flowering begins. Older leaves resist better and hotter midseason weather usually stops it.
source: Downy Mildew on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Downy Mildew what to do, treatment and control: Check upper young leaves for yellow spots and the underside for grey fuzz, mainly in humid weather. Bury infested residue after harvest where disease was severe. Do not keep seed from a field with heavily infected pods. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Downy Mildew on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Downy Mildew prevention: Plant resistant varieties; many sources of resistance exist. Rotate soybean with a non-bean crop for at least one year. Use clean seed.
source: Downy Mildew on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Downy Mildew when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if many plants show spots before flowering ends.
source: Downy Mildew on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Frog Eye Leaf Spot. A fungus disease of soybean that makes small spots with a reddish-brown or purple ring, like a frog's eye. It spreads in warm, humid weather and can cause leaf drop.
source: Frogeye Leaf Spot on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Frog Eye Leaf Spot symptoms: Small dark, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown or gray with a reddish-brown or purple ring. Older spot centres turn light gray or white with tiny black specks, or fall out leaving a shot-hole look. Spots can join into large damaged areas and leaves may drop early. Spots can also be on stems, pods and seed. Young leaves near the top are hit most.
source: Frogeye Leaf Spot on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Frog Eye Leaf Spot causes and spread: Caused by the fungus Cercospora sojina, which survives on crop residue and in seed. Rain splash carries spores from residue up to young leaves, and new spores form on the spots all season. Warm, humid and long wet spells favour it, usually after flowering. Infection at or before flowering causes the biggest loss; late infection matters little.
source: Frogeye Leaf Spot on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Frog Eye Leaf Spot what to do, treatment and control: Check young upper leaves for spots with reddish-brown or purple rings, from flowering onward. In fields with heavy disease, bury soybean residue; if that is not possible, rotate to another crop. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Do not save seed from a field with heavy disease.
source: Frogeye Leaf Spot on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Frog Eye Leaf Spot prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Use disease-free seed. Rotate soybean with a non-bean crop. Do not plant soybean into infested residue.
source: Frogeye Leaf Spot on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Frog Eye Leaf Spot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spots appear before or around flowering on susceptible varieties.
source: Frogeye Leaf Spot on Soybean - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Mosaic. A virus disease of soybean that mottles and crinkles the leaves. It can stunt plants and spoil seed quality. There is no cure once a plant is infected.
source: Soybean Mosaic Virus - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Mosaic symptoms: Leaves show light and dark green mottling, mostly on young fast-growing leaves. Leaf blades may pucker along the veins and curl downward, or look blistered and distorted. Infected plants may be stunted with fewer pods and smaller seeds. Seed can be mottled, which lowers grain quality and germination. Symptoms fade in very hot weather.
source: Soybean Mosaic Virus - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Mosaic causes and spread: Caused by Soybean mosaic virus, a virus that lives inside the plant. Infected seed is the most important way it enters a field. Aphids spread it from plant to plant, and it can also spread through plant sap. Plants infected when young show more symptoms.
source: Soybean Mosaic Virus - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Mosaic what to do, treatment and control: Use only clean seed; do not plant seed saved from fields where plants were mottled. Look for mottled, crinkled young leaves, and for aphids on the plants. Spraying for aphids does not reliably stop this virus; ask your agriculture officer before spending money on it.
source: Soybean Mosaic Virus - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Mosaic prevention: Plant seed that is free of the virus. Plant early, which may help. Choose varieties with some resistance where available.
source: Soybean Mosaic Virus - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Mosaic when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if many young plants show mottled, crinkled leaves.
source: Soybean Mosaic Virus - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Rust. A fast-spreading fungus disease of soybean that causes leaf spots and early leaf drop. Under favourable conditions it can cause very heavy yield loss.
source: Soybean Rust - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Rust symptoms: Tan or reddish-brown spots, first on the underside of lower leaves. Small blister-like pustules form in the spots, then burst and release tan spores. Spots and pustules can also be on pods and stems; a hand lens helps to see them. Heavy attack causes leaf drop.
source: Soybean Rust - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Rust causes and spread: Caused by the rust fungus Phakopsora pachyrhizi, which survives only on living green plants. Its spores are carried by wind, sometimes over long distances. Favoured by long wet weather, moderate temperatures and high humidity, and most common at and after flowering. Early spots, before pustules form, look like other common leaf diseases.
source: Soybean Rust - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Rust what to do, treatment and control: Check lower leaves every week, especially in wet weather after flowering starts. Look at the underside of leaves with a hand lens for pustules and tell your agriculture officer early. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Soybean Rust - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Rust prevention: Early scouting is the key. Early sowing in a season has been seen to suffer less damage in Indian trials. Ask your agriculture office which varieties are better for your area, since resistant ones are limited.
source: Soybean Rust - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Soybean Rust when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer at once if you see rusty spots on the underside of leaves.
source: Soybean Rust - University of Minnesota Extension

text: Tomato Bacterial Spot. A bacterial disease that makes small dark spots on tomato leaves and rough, scab-like blisters on fruit. It spreads fast in warm, wet, humid weather.
source: Bacterial diseases of tomato - University of Maryland Extension

text: Tomato Bacterial Spot symptoms: Small dark spots on leaves, sometimes water-soaked, with yellow tissue around them. Spots join into larger brown patches in warm, wet weather, and leaves may drop. Small raised blisters on fruit that grow and turn rough and scab-like. Heavy leaf loss leaves fruit open to sunscald.
source: Bacterial diseases of tomato - University of Maryland Extension

text: Tomato Bacterial Spot causes and spread: Bacteria of the Xanthomonas group cause the disease. They survive on crop residue and can be carried on seed and seedlings. Splashing rain, wet handling of plants, tools and hands spread the bacteria. Warm, wet, humid weather favours it; hot, dry weather slows it.
source: Bacterial diseases of tomato - University of Maryland Extension

text: Tomato Bacterial Spot what to do, treatment and control: Remove infected plants and seedlings and destroy all infected crop residue away from the field. Do not work among plants or handle them when the leaves are wet, so bacteria are not moved by hands and tools. Avoid watering over the leaves. Water at the base of the plant if you can. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Clean tools and trays used on infected plants before using them on healthy ones.
source: Bacterial diseases of tomato - University of Maryland Extension

text: Tomato Bacterial Spot prevention: Buy clean seed and healthy seedlings from a trusted supplier. Do not crowd plants, and mulch the soil around them. After the season, plough or bury crop residue and remove volunteer tomato and pepper plants. Rotate with crops that are not tomato or pepper for at least one year in fields that had the disease.
source: Bacterial diseases of tomato - University of Maryland Extension

text: Tomato Bacterial Spot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if spots spread quickly or you cannot tell this from other leaf spot diseases.
source: Bacterial diseases of tomato - University of Maryland Extension

text: Tomato Early Blight. A fungal leaf disease that shows as brown spots with ring patterns, first on the oldest leaves. It can kill leaves, damage fruit and cut yield.
source: Early Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Early Blight symptoms: Brown dead spots on the older, lower leaves, often with a yellow halo and ring-like marks like a target. Badly infected leaves turn yellow, wither and drop, which exposes fruit to sunscald. Leathery spots on fruit near the stem end. Dark stem spots on seedlings; infected seedlings may die or stay stunted.
source: Early Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Early Blight causes and spread: A fungus (Alternaria solani) that survives in infected plant debris in the soil and can also travel on seed. Spores spread by wind, rain splash and overhead water. Warm, wet weather, heavy dew and plants weakened by poor fertility, drought or heavy fruit load favour it.
source: Early Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Early Blight what to do, treatment and control: Remove and destroy badly infected leaves and plant debris, and do not leave them in the field. Scout older leaves every week, especially after rain or heavy dew, so you catch spots early. Pull out weeds and volunteer tomato, potato, eggplant and pepper plants that can carry the fungus. Keep plants healthy with good soil fertility and steady watering, because stressed plants get the disease more easily. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Early Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Early Blight prevention: Use clean, disease-free seed and healthy seedlings. Rotate away from tomato, potato, eggplant and pepper for at least 2 years. Choose varieties with some resistance where your seed supplier offers them. Plough or turn under crop debris after harvest to reduce spores near the next crop.
source: Early Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Early Blight when to get help: Ask your agriculture extension officer for help if leaf spotting keeps spreading despite removing infected leaves.
source: Early Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Late Blight. A very fast disease of tomato and potato, caused by a water mould, that can kill whole plants within days in cool, wet weather.
source: Late Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Late Blight symptoms: Water-soaked spots on leaves that grow quickly into large olive-green to brown patches. White fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves in humid or wet weather. Brown to black spots on stems, and firm brown spots on fruit. Plants may collapse so fast they look frost-damaged.
source: Late Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Late Blight causes and spread: A water mould (Phytophthora infestans), the same organism behind the Irish potato famine, causes it. It survives on infected potato tubers, cull piles, volunteer potato and tomato plants and nightshade weeds. Wind and wind-driven rain carry the spores far. Cool, wet and cloudy weather favours it; hot, dry weather is not suitable for it.
source: Late Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Late Blight what to do, treatment and control: Remove infected plants quickly, bag them and bury them deep or throw them away. Do not compost them. Scout the crop often in cool, wet or foggy weather, looking at both sides of leaves and at stems. Destroy volunteer potato plants, cull piles and nightshade-family weeds near the field. Stake plants and keep air moving through the crop so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Spraying works best before symptoms appear.
source: Late Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Late Blight prevention: Plant disease-free seedlings and certified seed potatoes; do not replant last year's tubers. Choose tomato varieties with late blight resistance when available. Avoid watering over the leaves. Disinfect stakes and cages before reuse.
source: Late Blight - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Late Blight when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer at once if you see these spots in cool, wet weather, because the disease spreads very fast.
source: Late Blight - Utah State University Extension
