text: Tomato Leaf Mold. A fungal disease that makes yellow patches on the upper leaf and olive-green mould underneath. It is mainly a problem in humid greenhouses and tunnels.
source: Tomato Leaf Mold - UMass Amherst

text: Tomato Leaf Mold symptoms: Pale green or yellow spots with unclear edges on the upper leaf surface. Olive-green mould on the underside of the leaf, under the yellow spots. Infected leaves curl, wither and may drop; symptoms start at the bottom of the plant and move up. Sometimes flowers die and fruit gets a dark leathery rot at the stem end.
source: Tomato Leaf Mold - UMass Amherst

text: Tomato Leaf Mold causes and spread: A fungus (Passalora fulva) that lives on plant debris and can come in on seed. Spores spread by wind, water splash, tools, workers and insects. High humidity (above about 85 percent) and long leaf wetness favour it, so it is most common in greenhouses and high tunnels.
source: Tomato Leaf Mold - UMass Amherst

text: Tomato Leaf Mold what to do, treatment and control: Remove and destroy infected plants or leaves and clear crop debris. Lower humidity: open vents, use fans if you have them, and avoid wetting the leaves. Stake and prune plants so air can move through them. Clean tools and the structure well between crops. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Tomato Leaf Mold - UMass Amherst

text: Tomato Leaf Mold prevention: Use clean seed from a trusted supplier. Remove crop residue after harvest. Choose resistant varieties when available. Rotate crops and move tunnels from time to time so the disease does not build up.
source: Tomato Leaf Mold - UMass Amherst

text: Tomato Leaf Mold when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if mould appears on many plants in your greenhouse or tunnel.
source: Tomato Leaf Mold - UMass Amherst

text: Tomato Mosaic Virus. A virus disease that mottles tomato leaves light and dark green and can distort them. There is no cure, and it spreads on hands, tools and seed, not by insects.
source: Tobacco Mosaic Virus and Tomato Mosaic Virus - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Mosaic Virus symptoms: Light green, yellow or white mottling on leaves, which can look like a nutrient problem. Leaves may be curled, fan-shaped or very narrow and stringy. Smaller plants and lower yield and fruit quality. Some fruit show yellow rings, brown sunken spots or browning inside.
source: Tobacco Mosaic Virus and Tomato Mosaic Virus - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Mosaic Virus causes and spread: Tobacco mosaic virus and tomato mosaic virus are closely related viruses with similar symptoms. They are not spread by insects. They spread on contaminated seed, hands, clothing, pruning tools and stakes, and enter through tiny wounds. They can last a very long time in plant debris, and hands that touched tobacco products can carry the virus.
source: Tobacco Mosaic Virus and Tomato Mosaic Virus - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Mosaic Virus what to do, treatment and control: Remove infected plants right away and do not compost them. A virus cannot be cured once the plant is infected. Clean tools that touched infected plants before using them on healthy plants. Wash hands, and avoid handling plants after using tobacco products. Do not save seed from infected plants, and use fresh pots, soil and string for each new planting. Control weeds and keep new plantings away from infected plants.
source: Tobacco Mosaic Virus and Tomato Mosaic Virus - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Mosaic Virus prevention: Use certified disease-free seed. Plant resistant varieties; check which virus is present first because some varieties resist only one. Handle plants as little as possible, especially when pruning and staking. Rotate crops.
source: Tobacco Mosaic Virus and Tomato Mosaic Virus - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Mosaic Virus when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer or plant clinic to confirm the virus, since other problems and herbicide damage look similar.
source: Tobacco Mosaic Virus and Tomato Mosaic Virus - Utah State University Extension

text: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot. A fungal disease that causes many small round spots on lower tomato leaves, which then yellow and fall. It rarely infects fruit, but leaf loss cuts yield.
source: Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato - University of Maine Cooperative Extension

text: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot symptoms: Small round spots on the lower leaves, with a dark border and a grey-white centre. Tiny black dots inside the spots, which are the fungus spore bodies. Heavily infected leaves yellow, wither and drop, starting from the bottom of the plant. Fruit are left open to sunscald after leaves fall.
source: Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato - University of Maine Cooperative Extension

text: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot causes and spread: A fungus (Septoria lycopersici) that survives on infected tomato and related plant debris and can travel on seed. Spores spread by rain splash, wind and people. Warm, wet weather, long leaf wetness and dense leaves that dry slowly favour it.
source: Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato - University of Maine Cooperative Extension

text: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot what to do, treatment and control: Hand-pick and destroy infected lower leaves to reduce spores. Do not work in the crop when the leaves are wet. Water early in the day and keep water off the leaves where possible. Stake plants and space them so air moves through the canopy. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato - University of Maine Cooperative Extension

text: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot prevention: Use disease-free seed. Remove and destroy crop debris at season end, or plough it under. Rotate away from tomato for about three years and control nightshade-type weeds. Keep plants well fed so they stay healthy.
source: Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato - University of Maine Cooperative Extension

text: Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if leaf loss spreads up the plant.
source: Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato - University of Maine Cooperative Extension

text: Tomato Spider Mites. Tiny sap-sucking mites that live under tomato leaves and cause speckling, yellowing and fine webbing. This is a pest problem, not an infection.
source: Tomato - Spider Mites - UConn Integrated Pest Management

text: Tomato Spider Mites symptoms: Fine white to yellow speckling on leaves, later turning bronze or brown. Tiny moving dots under the leaf; shake a leaf over white paper to see them. Fine webbing on leaf undersides and stems when numbers are high. Leaves yellow, dry out and drop, exposing fruit to sunscald.
source: Tomato - Spider Mites - UConn Integrated Pest Management

text: Tomato Spider Mites causes and spread: The two-spotted spider mite is a tiny, eight-legged mite that feeds on plant sap, mainly under leaves. It multiplies fastest in hot, dry, dusty weather and on drought-stressed plants, and is common in tunnels and greenhouses. High nitrogen in the leaves encourages it, and it also feeds on beans, cucumbers, peppers, eggplant and many other crops.
source: Tomato - Spider Mites - UConn Integrated Pest Management

text: Tomato Spider Mites what to do, treatment and control: Check the undersides of leaves often, especially under speckled areas, to catch mites early. Wash mites off with a strong stream of water. Protect natural enemies such as ladybird beetles, lacewings and predatory mites. Check new plants before bringing them into your field or tunnel. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Tomato - Spider Mites - UConn Integrated Pest Management

text: Tomato Spider Mites prevention: Keep plants healthy and avoid drought stress. Avoid too much nitrogen fertiliser. Start checking in hot weather. Avoid broad-spectrum sprays, which kill the natural enemies of mites.
source: Tomato - Spider Mites - UConn Integrated Pest Management

text: Tomato Spider Mites when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if webbing and leaf bronzing keep spreading.
source: Tomato - Spider Mites - UConn Integrated Pest Management

text: Tomato Target Spot. A fungal leaf disease that makes spots with ring patterns on tomato leaves, stems and fruit. It can cause heavy leaf loss in warm, wet weather.
source: Tomato target spot - Pacific Pests, Pathogens, Weeds and Pesticides

text: Tomato Target Spot symptoms: Small irregular spots with a yellow edge on the older, lower leaves. Some spots grow and show ring patterns like a target. Leaves yellow, collapse and die as the disease spreads to other leaves. Long thin spots on stems, and small light brown spots with dark edges on fruit.
source: Tomato target spot - Pacific Pests, Pathogens, Weeds and Pesticides

text: Tomato Target Spot causes and spread: A fungus (Corynespora cassiicola) that also infects papaya, cucumber and legumes and survives on old tomato crop remains. Rain carried by wind spreads the spores. Warm, wet weather and overhead watering favour it.
source: Tomato target spot - Pacific Pests, Pathogens, Weeds and Pesticides

text: Tomato Target Spot what to do, treatment and control: Remove and burn lower leaves as soon as the disease appears. Remove some lower branches so air can move at the base of the plant. Keep the plot free of weeds, which may host the fungus. Avoid overhead watering. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
source: Tomato target spot - Pacific Pests, Pathogens, Weeds and Pesticides

text: Tomato Target Spot prevention: Do not plant next to older diseased crops, and keep away from papaya if its leaves have small angular spots. Check seedlings in the nursery and discard any with leaf spots. Collect and burn crop residue after harvest. Wait at least 3 years before planting tomato again on the same land.
source: Tomato target spot - Pacific Pests, Pathogens, Weeds and Pesticides

text: Tomato Target Spot when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if the spots spread across the crop in wet weather.
source: Tomato target spot - Pacific Pests, Pathogens, Weeds and Pesticides

text: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus. A virus spread by whiteflies that makes young tomato leaves yellow and curled and the plant stunted. Plants infected young give little or no fruit.
source: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus - NC State Extension

text: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus symptoms: Yellowing of young leaves, between the veins and at the edges. Small crumpled leaves that curl up or down. Stunted, bushy plants with short spaces between leaves. Flowers drop before fruit set, so yield falls sharply.
source: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus - NC State Extension

text: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus causes and spread: A virus (a begomovirus) carried by the adult whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), which picks it up by feeding on infected plants. Infected plants without symptoms, such as transplants, can carry it over long distances. Other crops and weeds can also hold the virus. Symptoms can take up to three weeks to appear after infection.
source: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus - NC State Extension

text: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus what to do, treatment and control: Remove and destroy infected plants so whiteflies cannot carry the virus from them. Hang yellow or white sticky traps in and around the field and check leaf undersides for whitefly eggs and young. Use reflective mulch if available, because it keeps whiteflies away. Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly. Keep tomato away from other tomato, pepper and bean fields that may hold the virus.
source: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus - NC State Extension

text: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus prevention: Plant resistant varieties and healthy, clean seedlings. In nurseries and greenhouses, use whitefly-proof screens. Rotate with crops that do not host the virus. Check that nutrient problems are not the cause: they affect the whole crop evenly, while this virus appears in patches.
source: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus - NC State Extension

text: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus when to get help: Contact your agriculture extension officer to confirm the problem, because nutrient shortages and heat can look similar.
source: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus - NC State Extension
